newsitem.title: CHINA: CHINA RPI RISE SEEN SLOWED BY PRICE WAR, HARVESTS.
newsitem.headline: CHINA RPI RISE SEEN SLOWED BY PRICE WAR, HARVESTS.

text.p: A price war in China's consumer durables sector and bumper fruit and vegetable harvests tamed inflation in July, but strong economic growth could fuel prices rises in the last part of the year, analysts said on Wednesday.
Year-on-year July retail price inflation to slowed to 0.6 percent, down from 0.8 percent in June and May, official figures showed.
Qiu Xiaohua, head economist of the State Statistical Bureau, said increased supplies of seasonal fruits and vegetables on the market had brought down food prices, slowing overall inflation.
Fresh fruit prices tumbled 25.1 percent, fresh vegetables prices slipped 5.2 percent and grain prices shed 1.6 percent, the official Xinhua news agency quoted Statistical Bureau figures as saying.
China does not detail what is in the basket of goods used to calculate the retail price index or how they are weighted, but analysts believe food plays a key role.
Hong Kong economists said price drops were also being felt elsewhere as competition in the consumer durables sector heated up.

"You can see a lot of ad-hoc evidence that producers are losing their pricing power, with a price war in consumer durables that has spread to other sectors," said Qu Hongbin of Dresdner Kleinwort Benson Securities Hong Kong.
But a rebound in economic growth could push retail price inflation up to around 3.8 percent in 1997, said Joe Lo of Citibank Hong Kong.
"We're coming to expect (the index figures) a little higher. We expect more robust activity in the second half," he said.
Qiu predicted retail price inflation would stay below three percent in 1997, saying overall prices had stabilised.
China has predicted three- to four-percent retail price inflation this year, revised down from an earlier forecast for 6.0 percent.
Retail price inflation for January to July was 1.6 percent year-on-year. The index rose 6.1 percent in 1996, down from 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
